predecessors.note: The political predecessor is the French West Africa federation (french-africa dossier). The Ivory Coast page notes that 'the northern boundary was not fixed until 1947' after French efforts to attach parts of Upper Volta and French Sudan.

capitals.name: Abidjan
capitals.note: The page says only that 'Since 1983, Ivory Coast's capital has been Yamoussoukro, while Abidjan was the administrative centre'; Abidjan as capital before 1983 is the researcher's reading. Abidjan remains the economic centre.

capitals.name: Yamoussoukro
capitals.note: 'Since 1983, Ivory Coast's capital has been Yamoussoukro'; Abidjan, 'its largest city and economic centre', stays the administrative centre.

ledger.note: 7 August 1960: Côte d'Ivoire becomes independent from France. Infobox: 'Independence from France: 7 August 1960'.
1983: Yamoussoukro becomes the capital. 'Since 1983, Ivory Coast's capital has been Yamoussoukro, while Abidjan was the administrative centre.'

region.text: 'much of the north of the country', including 'the cities of Bouaké and Korhogo' (admin-1 units Savanes, Zanzan, Vallée du Bandama, Worodougou, Bafing, Denguélé and Dix-Huit Montagnes, from the zones centred on Bouna, Katiola, Bouaké, Mankono, Séguéla, Man and Touba: the researcher's mapping)

ledger.note: 19 September 2002: rebels seize the north. The war 'began with a military rebellion on 19 September 2002'; the rebels 'quickly established control over much of the north of the country', including Bouaké and Korhogo, a 'de facto partition' between a rebel-held north and a government-held south. A ceasefire followed on 17 October 2002 (Linas-Marcoussis Accord 26 January 2003; comprehensive ceasefire 3 May 2003). The extent is the researcher's mapping from the zones named on the Forces Nouvelles page.

region.text: 'much of the north of the country', including 'the cities of Bouaké and Korhogo' (admin-1 units Savanes, Zanzan, Vallée du Bandama, Worodougou, Bafing, Denguélé and Dix-Huit Montagnes, from the zones centred on Bouna, Katiola, Bouaké, Mankono, Séguéla, Man and Touba: the researcher's mapping)

ledger.note: 2011: the north returns to the state. Page silent on the date the rebel-held zones were handed back: the First Ivorian Civil War page gives the 4 March 2007 peace agreement, Gbagbo's 16 April 2007 declaration that the war was over and the full dismantling of the UN buffer zone in July 2008; the Forces Nouvelles page says only 'After the New Forces were mostly integrated into the Ivorian army in 2011', and the First Ivorian Civil War page that the second civil war ended with Gbagbo's defeat and arrest in April 2011. The year is a bridging judgment.

wars.name: First Ivorian Civil War

zones.text: 'much of the north of the country', including 'the cities of Bouaké and Korhogo' (admin-1 units Savanes, Zanzan, Vallée du Bandama, Worodougou, Bafing, Denguélé and Dix-Huit Montagnes, from the zones centred on Bouna, Katiola, Bouaké, Mankono, Séguéla, Man and Touba: the researcher's mapping)

wars.outcome: A ceasefire on 17 October 2002, the Linas-Marcoussis Accord on 26 January 2003 and the Ouagadougou agreement of 4 March 2007 ended the fighting; the rebel-held north and government-held south remained a 'de facto partition' until the New Forces were integrated.
wars.note: Infobox: 19 September 2002 - 4 March 2007, 'War agreement, followed by renewed conflict'. 'France sent in troops to maintain the cease-fire boundaries' and UN peacekeepers kept a buffer zone (Ivory Coast page); the page dates the full dismantling of the buffer zone to July 2008.

wars.name: Second Ivorian Civil War
wars.outcome: 'The second civil war ended with Gbagbo's defeat and arrest in April 2011.' The page gives no territorial division.
wars.note: The Ivory Coast page says 'The 2010 presidential election led to the 2010-2011 Ivorian crisis and the Second Ivorian Civil War.' Listed so the reviewer can see it was considered; the rebel-held north is already carried by the 2002 loss event.

certainty.note: Judgment: the frontier is inherited from the French delimitation ('the northern boundary was not fixed until 1947'); the pages give no later change. The 2002-2011 partition line between the rebel-held north and the south is soft.

notes: Budget: 3 pages (state, first civil war, and the Forces Nouvelles page for the rebel zones), one over the brief's 1-2; the Forces Nouvelles page is thin and was opened to name the zones. Cliopatria draws the whole country throughout. The rebel-held north 2002-2011 is carried by a loss and a gain against the rebel dossier 'forces-nouvelles-de-cote-d-ivoire' (written in this batch, type rebel). The extent is an admin-1 reading of the named zones; the front ran north of Yamoussoukro but no page gives the line, and the share of the country held is page silent. The 2011 return of the north is confidence 1: the pages give 2007 (agreement, war declared over), July 2008 (buffer zone dismantled) and 2011 (integration into the army, Gbagbo's defeat) but no date for the end of rebel administration; a gap-filler should open 'Ivorian Civil War' pages on the Second Ivorian Civil War and the 2011 Battle of Abidjan. Abidjan as the capital before 1983 is the researcher's reading. Gabon and Ivory Coast recognised Biafra in May 1968 (Nigerian Civil War page); the Ivory Coast page is silent. Neighbours in the seed: Burkina Faso, Ghana, Guinea, Mali Federation, Liberia.
